meta.subject: maths
meta.title: Areas Related to Circles
meta.source_edition: NCERT Reprint 2026-27, Class 10 Mathematics, Ch 11 (jemh111.pdf, printed pages 154-160)

board_asks: almost every mark here comes from three moves — the length of an arc, the area of a sector (the fraction θ/360 of the circle), and the area of a segment (that sector minus triangle OAB). Get the central angle and the value of π right, and know when to leave √3 in surd form. The 2026-27 chapter is trimmed to sectors and segments only — combinations of plane figures are no longer in it.

big_idea.tagline: A slice of the circle — measured by its angle.
big_idea.body: Every result in this chapter is one idea: a part of a circle is the fraction $\dfrac{\theta}{360}$ of the whole, where $\theta$ is the angle it makes at the centre. Take that fraction of the circumference $2\pi r$ and you get an arc length; take it of the area $\pi r^2$ and you get a sector; cut a chord across and the leftover piece is a segment, found by subtracting triangle $OAB$ from the sector.

definitions.verbatim: the portion (or part) of the circular region enclosed by two radii and the corresponding arc is called a sector of the circle
definitions.plain: A 'pizza slice' of the disc — the region boxed in by two radii and the arc between them, with its pointed corner at the centre $O$.

definitions.verbatim: the portion (or part) of the circular region enclosed between a chord and the corresponding arc is called a segment of the circle
definitions.plain: The region cut off by a straight chord and the arc it subtends — like the slice of melon left after one straight cut. No radius is involved.

definitions.verbatim: Area of a sector of a circle with radius r and angle with degree measure θ is (θ/360) × πr²
definitions.plain: Take the fraction $\dfrac{\theta}{360}$ of the whole circle's area $\pi r^2$. Convert the central angle to degrees first.

source.note: Summary point 2; the printed fraction is linearised with brackets (math region flagged by the fidelity gate)

definitions.term: Length of an arc of a sector
definitions.verbatim: Length of an arc of a sector of a circle with radius r and angle with degree measure θ is (θ/360) × 2πr
definitions.plain: The same fraction $\dfrac{\theta}{360}$, but of the whole circumference $2\pi r$ — the curved boundary of the sector, measured in length (cm), not area.

source.note: Summary point 1; the printed fraction is linearised (math region flagged by the fidelity gate)

definitions.verbatim: Area of segment of a circle = Area of the corresponding sector – Area of the corresponding triangle.
definitions.plain: There is no direct formula — always subtract: segment $=$ its sector $-$ triangle $OAB$. Finding the triangle (the chord and the perpendicular height) is the hard part.

definitions.verbatim: OAPB is called the minor sector and OAQB is called the major sector.
APB is called the minor segment and AQB is called the major segment.
∠ AOB is called the angle of the sector.
When we write 'segment' and 'sector' we will mean the 'minor segment' and the 'minor sector' respectively, unless stated otherwise.

concepts.title: Sector — minor and major
concepts.body: Two radii plus the arc between them cut the disc into two sectors. The smaller one (shaded, $OAPB$) is the minor sector and carries the angle $\theta = \angle AOB$; the larger one ($OAQB$) is the major sector with angle $360^\circ - \theta$.
concepts.tested: 2-mark 'find the area of the sector' (Section A/B)

concepts.title: Segment — minor and major
concepts.body: A chord $AB$ (not a radius) splits the disc into two segments. The piece between the chord and its arc is the minor segment ($APB$, shaded); the rest is the major segment ($AQB$). A segment always needs the triangle $OAB$ to measure it.
concepts.tested: 3-mark 'find the area of the segment' (Section C)

concepts.title: Length of an arc
concepts.body: The curved edge of a sector of angle $\theta$ is the fraction $\dfrac{\theta}{360}$ of the full circumference: $\ell = \dfrac{\theta}{360}\times 2\pi r$. It is a length (cm), so never square it.
concepts.tested: 1-2 mark direct, or part (i) of a case-based problem

concepts.title: Area of a sector
concepts.body: The same fraction, taken of the area: $\dfrac{\theta}{360}\times \pi r^2$. For the major sector the fast route is $\pi r^2 - (\text{minor sector})$, which avoids re-substituting $360^\circ-\theta$.
concepts.tested: 2-3 mark direct 'find the area of the sector'

concepts.title: Area of a segment = sector − triangle
concepts.body: There is no direct formula. Area of the minor segment $= \dfrac{\theta}{360}\times\pi r^2 - \text{area of }\triangle OAB$. Get the triangle from a perpendicular dropped from $O$ to the chord (using $\cos$ and $\sin$ of half the angle), or — when $\theta = 60^\circ$ — as an equilateral triangle of side $r$.

examples.shape: Area of a sector + major sector · NCERT Example 1
examples.problem_verbatim: Find the area of the sector of a circle with radius 4 cm and of angle 30°. Also, find the area of the corresponding major sector (Use π = 3.14).

solution_steps.text: Area of the major sector $= \pi r^2 - 4.19 = 3.14\times 16 - 4.19 = 46.05 \approx 46.1\ \text{cm}^2$ (approx.).

examples.mark_logic: 3-mark shape: 1 for the sector formula with correct substitution, 1 for the minor-sector value $4.19\text{ cm}^2$, 1 for the major sector via $\pi r^2 - \text{minor}$. NCERT also gives the alternative $\dfrac{360-30}{360}\pi r^2$ route — either earns the last mark.

examples.shape: Area of a sector · NCERT Exercise 11.1 Q1
examples.problem_verbatim: Find the area of a sector of a circle with radius 6 cm if angle of the sector is 60°.

solution_steps.lead: Substitute into the sector formula (π = 22/7 by default).

examples.mark_logic: 2-mark shape: 1 for substituting into $\dfrac{\theta}{360}\pi r^2$ with $\pi=\dfrac{22}{7}$ (the exercise's default), 1 for the simplified answer $\dfrac{132}{7}\text{ cm}^2$ with unit.

source.note: exercise question; NCERT leaves it unsolved — the step-marked solution here is authored to the CBSE scheme

examples.shape: Area of a segment · NCERT Example 2
examples.problem_verbatim: Find the area of the segment AYB shown in Fig. 11.6, if radius of the circle is 21 cm and ∠ AOB = 120°. (Use π = 22/7)

solution_steps.text: Area of segment $AYB = $ Area of sector $OAYB - $ Area of $\triangle OAB$. Sector $OAYB = \dfrac{120}{360}\times\dfrac{22}{7}\times 21^2 = 462\ \text{cm}^2$.

solution_steps.lead: Drop OM ⊥ AB and use the half-angle.
solution_steps.text: $OA = OB$, so by RHS congruence $M$ is the mid-point of $AB$ and $\angle AOM = \angle BOM = 60^\circ$. Then $OM = OA\cos 60^\circ = \dfrac{21}{2}$ and $AM = OA\sin 60^\circ = \dfrac{21\sqrt{3}}{2}$, so $AB = 2AM = 21\sqrt{3}$.

examples.mark_logic: Long-answer shape (4 marks): 1 for the sector area $462\text{ cm}^2$ and the 'sector − triangle' setup, 1 for the perpendicular construction giving $OM$ and $AB$, 1 for the triangle area $\dfrac{441\sqrt3}{4}\text{ cm}^2$, 1 for the final subtracted answer. Leaving $\sqrt3$ in surd form is correct here — no value of $\sqrt3$ is given.

source.note: problem on p.157; solution runs to p.158

examples.shape: Area swept by a minute hand (arc application) · NCERT Exercise 11.1 Q3
examples.problem_verbatim: The length of the minute hand of a clock is 14 cm. Find the area swept by the minute hand in 5 minutes.

solution_steps.lead: Turn the time into a central angle.
solution_steps.text: The minute hand sweeps $360^\circ$ in $60$ minutes, so in $5$ minutes it turns $\dfrac{5}{60}\times 360^\circ = 30^\circ$. The area swept is a sector of radius $r = 14$ cm and angle $30^\circ$.

examples.mark_logic: 3-mark shape: 1 for converting 5 minutes to a $30^\circ$ central angle (the step most students skip), 1 for substituting into $\dfrac{\theta}{360}\pi r^2$, 1 for the simplified $\dfrac{154}{3}\text{ cm}^2$ with unit.

source.note: exercise question; NCERT leaves it unsolved — the step-marked solution here is authored to the CBSE scheme (π = 22/7 by the exercise default)

examples.shape: Arc length + sector + segment · NCERT Exercise 11.1 Q5
examples.problem_verbatim: In a circle of radius 21 cm, an arc subtends an angle of 60° at the centre. Find: (i) the length of the arc (ii) area of the sector formed by the arc (iii) area of the segment formed by the corresponding chord

solution_steps.text: Two radii with a $60^\circ$ angle make $\triangle OAB$ equilateral of side $21$, so its area $= \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}\times 21^2 = \dfrac{441\sqrt{3}}{4}\ \text{cm}^2$. Segment $= $ sector $-$ triangle $= \left(231 - \dfrac{441\sqrt{3}}{4}\right)\ \text{cm}^2$.

examples.mark_logic: 3-mark shape (one per part): 1 for the arc length $22\text{ cm}$, 1 for the sector area $231\text{ cm}^2$, 1 for the segment as sector minus the equilateral triangle $OAB$. The $60^\circ$ angle making $\triangle OAB$ equilateral is the key insight in (iii).

source.note: exercise question; NCERT leaves it unsolved — the step-marked solution here is authored to the CBSE scheme (π = 22/7 by the exercise default; √3 left in surd form as no value is given)

strategies.text: All three start from the fraction $\dfrac{\theta}{360}$. Multiply it by $2\pi r$ for an arc (length), by $\pi r^2$ for a sector (area).
There is no direct formula — compute sector $-$ triangle $OAB$. Find the triangle separately.
Two radii with a $60^\circ$ angle make an equilateral triangle — its area is $\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}a^2$ with $a = r$.
Major $=$ whole $-$ minor: $\pi r^2 - (\text{minor sector})$, or $\pi r^2 - (\text{minor segment})$. Or use the angle $360^\circ - \theta$.
Use what the question states — $\dfrac{22}{7}$ by default in this exercise, $3.14$ when told. Keep $\sqrt{3}$ in surd form unless a value is given.

pitfalls.text: Reaching for a 'segment formula' — there isn't one. A segment is always sector $-$ triangle $OAB$.
Forgetting to turn a time / fraction into a central angle — 5 minutes on a clock is $30^\circ$, not $5^\circ$.
Mixing up arc length ($\times 2\pi r$) with sector area ($\times \pi r^2$) — check the unit: cm for an arc, cm$^2$ for an area.
Rounding π early or dropping the unit — state cm$^2$ and keep $\sqrt{3}$ exact unless a numerical value is supplied.

third_tab_content.name: Where the sector, arc and segment formulae come from
third_tab_content.intro: NCERT derives all three results by the Unitary Method (pp.155-156): scale the whole circle down by the fraction of the angle at the centre. This is the reasoning behind the formulae in the formula strip — worth understanding, not just memorising.

steps.claim: A full circle subtends 360° at the centre, and the area of the circular region is πr².
Unitary Method: when the angle at the centre is 360° the sector area is πr², so when the angle is 1° the sector area is πr²/360.
Therefore for an angle θ at the centre, the sector area is θ times the 1° value.
steps.math: $\text{Area of the sector of angle }\theta = \dfrac{\theta}{360}\times \pi r^2$
steps.justification: This is the area-of-a-sector formula (NCERT p.155).

steps.claim: The same Unitary-Method argument on the whole circumference 2πr (which corresponds to 360°) gives the arc length.
steps.math: $\text{length of an arc of angle }\theta = \dfrac{\theta}{360}\times 2\pi r$

steps.claim: The minor segment is what remains of the sector after triangle OAB is removed, so its area is the sector minus that triangle.
steps.justification: NCERT p.156 — segment = sector − corresponding triangle.
